title: Security awareness and suspicious behaviour
siteNotes: Who the manager on duty is and how to reach them quickly, including at weddings and events.
The venue's evacuation and invacuation points and how staff are told, and where guests go if the building must be cleared (links to the fire safety session).
Where lost property and the cloakroom or bag drop are, and how found items are logged.
Which areas are staff-only and how doors and keys are controlled.
Whether Martyn's Law applies to the venue (it depends on capacity, so the GM needs to confirm the figure used and when duties start) and who is responsible for the venue's plan.
How staff access the free ACT Awareness e-learning and how completion is recorded.
legalNotes: HOT: Hidden, Obviously suspicious, Typical. NPSA / ACT guidance for deciding whether an unattended item is suspicious. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/crowded-places-guidance and https://www.protectuk.police.uk. NOT re-fetched this session; stated from NPSA and ACT materials.

Run Hide Tell: Counter Terrorism Policing / NPSA guidance on what to do in a firearms or weapons attack. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/stay-safe-film. Wording summarised, not quoted. Not re-fetched this session.

Suspicious behaviour and reporting: report to police on 101, or the Anti-Terrorist Hotline on 0800 789 321, or online at https://www.gov.uk/ACT; call 999 if there is a threat to life or an immediate risk. Numbers from Counter Terrorism Policing public guidance; not re-verified this session.

Martyn's Law is the Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025. It received Royal Assent on 3 April 2025. The government has said duties will not start straight away: there is an implementation period (reported as at least 24 months) while the Security Industry Authority prepares as regulator and statutory guidance is published. Reported from Protect UK and council pages and a search of gov.uk; the gov.uk factsheet page could not be opened. Reported capacity tiers: standard duty premises 200 to 799, enhanced duty 800 or more. Slides say only that it is being phased in and that the manager will say whether and when it applies to the venue. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/terrorism-protection-of-premises-act-2025

ACT Awareness e-learning: free, from Counter Terrorism Policing, takes about 45 minutes. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/act-awareness-elearning (page not re-checked). The slide says 'free' and 'worth doing' only; length not stated in slides.
Duty of care to staff and others: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 s.2 and s.3.
Not stated: any penalties, venue capacity figures, or staff legal duties under Martyn's Law.

Review Oct 2026: Martyn's Law position re-checked via secondary sources (FBHVC, Sheffield council, safety consultancies): Royal Assent 3 April 2025; implementation period of at least 24 months, duties expected spring 2027; SIA regulator; standard tier 200 to 799 expected capacity, enhanced 800+. Slides still say only 'phased in' and leave applicability to management. If the venue's wedding or function capacity is 200 or more it is likely to be in scope: GM to confirm capacity and the date duties start. HOT, Run Hide Tell and the reporting numbers were not re-fetched; they are unchanged standard counter-terrorism policing guidance.

cards.title: Security awareness and suspicious behaviour
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- decide whether an unattended item is suspicious using HOT
- spot and report suspicious behaviour
- know what to do in a serious incident: Run, Hide, Tell

cards.title: You know our building best
cards.body:
Our guests and wedding parties come and go all day. Staff are the people who know what looks normal here, and what does not.

Most things that seem odd turn out to be nothing. Spotting them and reporting them calmly is still the right thing to do.

items.title: Notice
items.text: What looks out of place for here?

items.title: Report
items.text: Tell your manager. Better safe than sorry.

cards.title: HOT: is it suspicious?
cards.body: A bag left behind is usually just forgotten. Ask HOT. If the answer to any one looks wrong, treat it as suspicious.

items.title: Obviously suspicious
items.text: Wires, batteries, odd smell, or looks like a threat?

items.title: Typical
items.text: Is it what you would expect to find here?

cards.title: What to do with a bag left behind
cards.body:
If it seems ordinary and typical, ask nearby guests and staff whose it is. If you cannot find an owner or it seems wrong, do not touch it. Move people away and tell your manager.

If you think it is dangerous, call 999.

left.title: Do
items: Call 999 if you think it is dangerous

right.title: Do not
items: Ignore it because it is busy

cards.title: Suspicious behaviour
cards.body:
Look for behaviour that does not fit: someone paying unusual attention to entrances, cameras or staff routines, taking photos of back-of-house areas, asking odd questions about security, or trying to get into staff-only areas.

Stay polite, do not confront, and tell your manager. A weak excuse is worth noting.

items: Leaving an item and walking off

cards.title: Run, Hide, Tell
cards.body:
If there is an attack with a weapon:
- **Run** if there is a safe route. Leave your belongings and help others if you can.
- **Hide** if you cannot get away. Lock or block the door, silence your phone, stay quiet.
- **Tell** the police on 999 when it is safe.

items.title: Run
items.text: Get away if it is safe. Do not wait for others.

items.title: Hide
items.text: Out of sight, door secured, phone silent.

items.title: Tell
items.text: Call 999: where, what, how many, descriptions.

cards.title: New law, being phased in
cards.body:
Martyn's Law is the Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025. It will require certain venues to plan how they would protect people from terrorism. It is being brought in in stages, not all at once.

Whether and when it applies to us is for the management. Your manager will show you what the venue's plan means for you. Everything in this session is good practice now.

items.title: Phased in
items.text: Duties do not all start at once

items.title: Free training
items.text: The ACT Awareness e-learning costs nothing

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Use HOT: Hidden, Obviously suspicious, Typical.
- Never touch a suspicious item. Keep people back and tell your manager.
- Report odd behaviour calmly. Do not confront.
- In a serious incident: Run, Hide, Tell. Call 999.

cards.q: During a wedding reception you find a holdall under a table in the corridor. Nobody nearby owns it. A wire is poking out of the top. What do you do?
options: Open it and look inside for a name or label
Move it carefully to lost property for the owner
Do not touch it; keep people back and tell your manager
Ask nearby guests to keep an eye on it for you
cards.why: A wire is an Obviously suspicious sign. Do not touch it. Keep people away and tell your manager, and call 999 if you believe it is dangerous.

cards.q: In HOT, the T stands for 'Typical', meaning whether the item is what you would expect to find in that place.
cards.why: Hidden, Obviously suspicious, Typical. A coat in the cloakroom is typical. The same bag hidden behind a bin is not.

cards.q: A man has asked you twice how often the back door is checked and has taken photos of the staff entrance. He says he is 'just interested in the architecture'. What now?
options: Tell him to leave straight away
Tell your manager, calmly, without confronting him
Take no notice, he gave a reason
Ask other guests what they think
cards.why: Odd interest in security and staff areas is worth reporting. Do not confront. Give your manager the facts and let them decide.

cards.q: Someone in the bar starts attacking guests with a weapon. The door to the car park is clear and close to you. What is your best first move?
options: Hide behind the bar until the person has gone
Run out of the door if it is safe, leaving your things
Stay where you are and try to calm him down
Phone your manager first so they know what is happening
cards.why: Run if there is a safe route. If you cannot get away, hide. Call 999 when it is safe to do so.

cards.q: Which TWO statements about Martyn's Law are accurate?
options: It started for every venue on the day it was passed
It is being phased in
Whether it applies depends on the premises, so the manager will say
It means every member of staff must carry security equipment
It replaces the fire safety rules
cards.why: The law is being phased in, and the management decides how it applies to the venue. It does not replace fire safety, nor ask staff to carry equipment.

cards.q: A coat and bag are left on a chair near the cloakroom after an event, as is common. Under HOT, what is the likely assessment?
options: Obviously suspicious, so clear the area and call 999
Typical for the place, so ask around for the owner
Hidden, as the bag was left out of sight
A reason to evacuate the building straight away
cards.why: Typical items in typical places are usually forgotten property. Ask around, and escalate if no one claims it or something looks wrong.

cards.q: If you think an item is suspicious you should pick it up to check inside.
cards.why: Never touch a suspicious item. Keep people back and tell your manager.

cards.q: In a serious incident, you cannot get away safely. What is the next best option?
options: Hide out of sight, with the door secured and phone silent
Stand in the open and watch what the attacker does
Go and look for the attacker to see where they are
Phone friends and family to tell them what is happening
cards.why: Run if you can, hide if you cannot, and tell the police when it is safe.

cards.q: Someone is trying door handles in the staff corridor and says they are looking for the toilets. What do you do?
options: Politely guide them back, then tell your manager
Ignore it, as they said they were after the toilets
Tackle them and hold them until the police arrive
Lock them in the corridor until a manager arrives
cards.why: Be polite and do not confront. Guide them back to the public area and tell your manager.

cards.q: What is the free training the session suggests for an extra layer of awareness?
options: ACT Awareness e-learning
A first aid course
A food hygiene course
A licensing exam
cards.why: The ACT Awareness e-learning is free and a good addition to this session.
